title: Distinguishing Majorana zero modes from trivial defect states on the surface of the iron-based superconductor Fe(Te,Se)
authors: Dongfei Wang, Jon Ortuzar, Freek Massee, Ruidan Zhong, Genda Gu, Wende Xiao, Yugui Yao, Roland Wiesendanger
abstract: Majorana zero modes, which obey non-Abelian exchange statistics, are promising candidates for topological quantum computation due to their robustness against environmental perturbations. The iron-based superconductor Fe(Te,Se) has been identified as an intrinsic topological superconductor, possibly hosting Majorana zero modes. In this paper, we report the observation of near-zero-energy localized states at multiple structural defects on the Fe(Te,Se) surface, which could be misidentified as Majorana zero modes without additional verification. By using spin-polarized scanning tunneling spectroscopy, we demonstrate that the near-zero-energy localized states on step edges and line defects originate from topologically trivial Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states. In addition, zero-energy bound states are also observed for regions without surface defects. A combined spatial and magnetic field dependent analysis of the spin-resolved tunneling spectra in these regions reveals that this type of zero-energy states cannot be attributed to the presence of Majorana bound states. These findings emphasize the importance of spin-dependent studies of low-energy states for pursuing Majorana zero modes.
summary: This work investigates whether near-zero-energy states observed on the surface of an iron-based superconductor are true Majorana zero modes, crucial for topological quantum computing. Using spin-polarized STM, the researchers analyzed defects and found that the spectral signatures are consistently explained by trivial Yu-Shiba-Rusinov bound states rather than robust topological edge modes.
main_problem: The central goal is to experimentally distinguish between true Majorana zero modes (MZMs) and topologically trivial defect states observed on the surface of an iron-based superconductor.
main_result: Through detailed spin-polarized scanning tunneling spectroscopy, the authors conclude that the observed near-zero-energy localized states at various defects are better explained by Yu-Shiba-Rusinov bound states originating from unpaired electrons rather than true topological Majorana modes.
method: The study employs advanced Scanning Tunneling Microscopy/Spectroscopy (STM/STS), including spin polarization measurements, to map the density of states across different surface defects like step edges and line defects.
model_or_system: The physical system is the iron-based superconductor Fe(Te,Se). The analysis involves comparing measured spectroscopic signatures against theoretical models describing YSR bound states coupled by magnetic impurities.
key_observables: Near-zero-energy localized states (Zero-Bias Peaks), spin polarization of the density of states ($	ext{SP-STS}$), and spectral weight transfer between positive and negative energies.
important_parameters: Temperature, external magnetic field strength (up to 3 T), and tunneling bias voltage ($V_{	ext{bias}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that true topological modes would exhibit specific signatures (e.g., dispersing behavior or unique spin dependence) which were not consistently found.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate various defect types on the surface, showing $	ext{d}I/	ext{d}V$ maps and line spectra taken across step edges, wrinkles, and bends to characterize in-gap states.
paper_structure: The paper systematically examines different classes of defects (step edges, Type I/II line defects) using STS. It progresses from initial observation of zero-bias peaks to detailed analysis involving spin polarization and comparison with established theoretical models for trivial bound states.
why_interesting: While not directly focused on AMO systems, the rigorous experimental methodology—using local probes (STM) combined with quantum mechanical diagnostics (spin/energy resolution)—provides a template for identifying exotic quasiparticles in condensed matter systems relevant to open quantum systems research.
